title: How to Evaluate Phone Policies in Schools
author: Jonathan Haidt
summary: Haidt releases a toolkit for assessing phone policies in schools, addressing a question teachers and administrators increasingly face: what policy actually works? The toolkit moves past binary bans-or-free-for-all and offers frameworks to evaluate policies based on school context, student needs, and implementation capacity. Phone policies exist on a spectrum: no phones allowed, phones stored during class, phones used for specified purposes, or no restrictions. Each has trade-offs. A genuine restrictive policy requires infrastructure (phone lockers, enforcement protocols) and culture shift (students and teachers must buy in). Half-measures produce resentment without benefit. The toolkit asks: What problem are we solving? What is the developmental stage of our student body? What staff capacity exists to enforce this? The evidence is clear: phones distract students, harm attention, and degrade academic outcomes when present in classrooms. But blanket bans backfire if students perceive them as unfair or if teachers lack capacity to enforce them. Schools that succeed with restrictions have done the cultural work: principal leadership, teacher buy-in, and clear communication about why the policy exists. Schools that try lightweight restrictions (students choose to put phones away, or phone-free zones in the library) often see minimal impact because the stakes feel low. Haidt's toolkit shifts the conversation from ideology to evidence and from compliance to coherent implementation.
points: Phone policies exist on a spectrum, and the right choice depends on school context, student developmental stage, and staff capacity to implement and enforce.
Half-measures backfire: a phone policy only works if students and teachers genuinely buy in and see it as coherent with school values.
Phones harm attention and academic outcomes, but the damage is reversible when clear policies are implemented with principal leadership and teacher support.
The key question is not whether to ban phones but how to implement a policy that your school can actually sustain and that students perceive as fair and purposeful.
Schools succeed with phone restrictions when they have done the cultural work: clear communication about why the policy exists and shared understanding of its purpose.
